q: To pass PSY113, which combination of results is required?
opts: At least 30% (of 60%) in CA and at least 20% (of 40%) in FA, with every assessment attempted
At least 50% overall, regardless of CA and FA
At least 20% in the final exam only
why: The course requires passing both CA (30/60) and FA (20/40), and all assessments are must-attempt (at least 20% each).

q: Aisha passed her Continuous Assessment but failed the Final Assessment. All assessments were attempted. What happens?
opts: She receives an FL grade and retakes the whole subject
She passes because CA is worth more
She receives a remedial grade and retakes the failed assessment next semester
She must redo all the assignments only
why: Failing only one of CA or FA leads to a remedial grade; FL is for failing both or not attempting an assessment.

q: How many tutorials must a student attend to avoid being barred from the final exam?
why: 80% attendance, i.e. 4 of the 5 tutorials, is required.

q: According to Lecture 1, science is an approach to knowing that relies on:
why: The lecture defines science as relying on observation, testing and falsification.

q: Which of the following is a NON-scientific question?
opts: How does sleep deprivation affect cognitive performance?
Does spending money on others promote happiness?
What is the purpose of my life?
Which drugs are most effective in managing depression?
why: Non-scientific questions are philosophical and subjective and cannot be tested with the scientific method.

q: Which statement about certainty in science is consistent with Lecture 1?
opts: Well-replicated findings in psychology are absolutely certain
No claim in science is absolutely certain, especially in psychology
Scientific knowledge is certain once peer reviewed
Certainty depends only on the researcher's reputation
why: Knowledge from the scientific method is based on a degree of certainty; no claim is absolutely certain.

q: In the basic scientific method, what step comes directly after doing background research?
why: The sequence is ask a question, background research, construct hypotheses, test/collect data, analyse, report.

q: A researcher reads a recent journal article, spots a weak argument, and designs a new study to test an alternative explanation. In Lecture 1's terms, she is:
why: Critiquing weak findings and building on them with a new study are ways of contributing to the scientific conversation.

q: Someone replies to 'more sleep leads to better mental functioning' with 'Koalas sleep 22 hours a day!' This reply is an example of:
opts: A nonsensical conversation, because it is not relevant
A good argument backed by evidence
why: In a scientific conversation each contribution must be new AND relevant; the koala reply is off-topic.

q: 'Higher hours of sleep, good sleep quality and strong social support lead to better mental health functioning.' How many variables are in this statement?
why: Hours of sleep, sleep quality, social support and mental health functioning are four variables.

q: Students who eat breakfast tend to have higher grades, but the researcher cannot say breakfast causes higher grades. This is a:
why: A non-causal relationship means two variables are related but one cannot be said to cause the other.

q: Which is a research question about a CAUSAL relationship?
opts: Is there a relationship between self-esteem and academic grades?
Can caffeine increase levels of attention?
What is the meaning of life?
Participants who drink coffee will sleep worse.
why: 'Can caffeine increase attention?' asks whether one variable causes change in another; the last option is a hypothesis, not a question.

q: 'Participants who drink coffee 3 hours before bedtime will have poorer sleep quality than those who don't.' This statement is best described as a:
why: A hypothesis is a prediction about the expected relationship between variables.

q: According to Lecture 1, what is a simple way to start familiarizing yourself with journal articles?
why: The lecture suggests starting by reading the abstract, and learning the standard journal structure.

q: Which describes excellence in writing DURING and AFTER university, rather than in school?
opts: Accurate rote memorisation of what others say
Thinking critically, deriving your own conclusions and communicating reasoning clearly
why: University writing means writing as professionals-to-be who question and critique and justify their reasoning.

q: 'You are not writing a science fiction novel. Get to the point!' describes which quality of good scientific writing?
why: Precise and succinct writing gets to the point and uses precise terms.

q: During a debate, Ben starts shouting and calls his opponent ignorant. According to Lecture 1:
opts: Ben has made a strong argument
Ben has already lost the argument
Ben is participating in the scientific conversation
why: Arguments are not verbal fights; raising your voice or making personal attacks means you have already lost.

q: Which argument would best support the claim that depression may partly be due to genetic factors?
opts: My neighbour and friend have depression, and so do their mothers
A research review found 70% of Malaysians with depression have a directly related family member diagnosed with depression
My father had depression, so it is definitely genetic
Many people believe depression runs in families
why: A good argument relies on research evidence from a larger sample rather than personal anecdotes.

q: Which source is a type of scholarly literature you can safely use as a main reference in a PSY113 assignment?
opts: A blog post by a psychologist
A Wikipedia page with many references
why: Journal articles are scholarly, peer-reviewed literature; blogs, wikis and magazines are not scientific literature.

q: A paper collects new survey data from 300 students and analyses it to test whether sleep predicts GPA. This is a(n):
why: Empirical articles present new, usually primary data, analysed to test hypotheses.

q: An author proposes a new model of motivation built from existing findings, without collecting any new data. This is a:
why: Theoretical/conceptual articles present a model based on existing findings, with no new data.

q: A systematic review and a meta-analysis are both forms of which type of journal article?
why: Review articles summarise a field and may be either a systematic review or a meta-analysis.

q: Compared with academic books, journal articles are more likely to:
opts: Cover broad topics and give a historical overview
Contain the latest findings and detailed methodology
Give only brief mention of methods
why: Journal articles are more focused, more recent, peer-reviewed to a high standard and detail their methodology.

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the criteria peer reviewers judge?
opts: The author's popularity on social media
why: Reviewers judge novelty, methods, consistency of results, strength of arguments, and language/grammar.

q: Why is the Wakefield et al. (1998) paper used as a case study in Lecture 2?
opts: It shows the harm when poorly controlled, conflicted research reaches the public before proper vetting
It is the best example of a meta-analysis
It shows that retractions happen within weeks
why: The poorly controlled MMR–autism study with an undisclosed conflict of interest took 12 years to retract, showing why vetting matters.

q: A tobacco company publishes a report finding its products do not cause lung cancer. According to Lecture 2, the main concern is that:
opts: It was published in a journal
There may be financial interests informing the research
why: White/policy papers are not peer-reviewed and may be driven by personal or financial agendas.

q: Information literacy is best described as:
opts: The ability to know what information is needed and to locate, evaluate and use it effectively
Accepting what experts say as absolute truth
why: Lecture 2 defines information literacy as knowing what information is needed and locating, evaluating and using it.

q: Which section of an empirical paper should be detailed enough for other researchers to replicate the study?
why: The Method section describes design, sample, measures and procedure in enough detail for replication.

q: In which section would you expect to find a non-statistical interpretation of results, limitations and suggestions for future studies?
why: The Discussion interprets results non-technically, notes limitations, and suggests future studies and implications.

q: The part of the introduction that explains how and why the variables are related, and that informs the hypotheses, is the:
why: The theoretical framework explains how and why variables are connected and informs the hypotheses.

q: 'Anxiety is a state of apprehension about future threats.' This is an example of a(n):
why: Conceptual definitions describe what a variable means; operational definitions describe how it is measured.

q: A study measures creativity as the total score on the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking (TTCT). This is a(n):
why: An operational definition states how a variable is measured, e.g. total TTCT score.

q: An article does not label its hypotheses. Which phrase would most likely signal a hypothesis?
opts: 'We predicted that women at peak fertility would…'
why: When hypotheses are not explicit, look for words like 'expect', 'predict' and 'hypothesize'.

q: In the Beall and Tracy (2013) article, the variables identified in the lecture are:
why: The lecture identifies shirt colour and fertility as the study's variables.

q: Which part of the Method section tells you who was included and excluded from a study?
why: The Sample describes who participated, their characteristics, and inclusion/exclusion.

q: The abstract of an empirical paper is best described as:
opts: A brief 150–250 word summary of the report
A list of the references used
why: Lecture 2 describes the abstract as a brief 150–250 word summary of the report.

q: A paper states: 'People who sleep less have weaker self-control because sleep loss depletes the glucose the prefrontal cortex needs to regulate impulses; therefore we predict a negative relationship between sleep debt and self-control.' Which part of the paper is this?
opts: The operational definitions in the Methods
why: It explains how and why two variables are connected to justify a hypothesis, which is what a theoretical framework is.

q: A paper states: 'Consistent with Hypothesis 2, loneliness significantly predicted depressive symptoms, r = .41, p < .001.' Which part of the paper is this?
why: The Results section reports the outcomes of statistical tests and whether each hypothesis is supported.

q: A paper states: 'Because our sample consisted only of undergraduate students, the findings may not generalise to older adults; future studies should test working adults.' This belongs to which purpose of the Discussion?
opts: Limitations and directions for future research
why: Acknowledging weaknesses and suggesting what future research should focus on is the limitations and future research purpose.

q: A paper states: 'These findings suggest school counsellors could introduce short mindfulness sessions before exams to reduce test anxiety.' What is this?
why: Practical implications concern real-world applications: who benefits and how the findings can be applied.

q: A paper states: 'Our results extend self-determination theory by showing that autonomy matters even in collectivist cultures.' What is this?
why: Theoretical implications describe how a study supports, challenges or extends existing psychological theories.

q: A student's Assignment 1 says the theoretical framework of an article is: 'The authors used evolutionary theory.' According to the lecture, what is wrong with this?
opts: Nothing; naming the theory is enough
A framework must always be labelled as a 'model' in the article
Listing a theory without explaining how and why the variables connect is not a theoretical framework
The framework should be taken from the Results section
why: A theoretical framework is not the same as a theory; simply listing a theory without explanation does not make it a framework.

q: A literature review lists five studies that all found a link between exercise and mood, but never says why the two are connected. What is missing?
opts: A theoretical framework explaining how and why the variables are related
why: A summary of past results does not tell you how variables are related; the framework must give the explanation.

q: A paper's Discussion opens: 'As predicted, students who journalled daily reported lower stress than controls, supporting Hypothesis 1; Hypothesis 2 was not supported.' Which purpose of the Discussion is this?
opts: Limitations and directions for future research
why: The summary of results restates the key findings and briefly says which hypotheses were supported.

q: In the 'how does water become ice?' example, why is Explanation 1 more convincing than 'water turns into ice at 0°C or below'?
opts: It explains the mechanism (molecules losing energy and sticking together)
why: A good framework explains how and why, not just restating that one thing follows another.

q: In the lecture's smartphone example, which theory explains why smartphone use may lower life satisfaction?
why: People use smartphones for social media, make unfavourable comparisons with others, and feel envy and dissatisfaction.

q: A Results section reports a statistically significant difference, but the difference between groups is tiny. Why does the lecture say the Results section is still worth reading closely?
opts: It tells you the article was peer reviewed
It gives details about the strength/magnitude of the effect
It gives the author's own opinion
why: Results give the strength/magnitude of an effect, which matters because some effects or relationships are very weak.

q: A Results section reports p = .03 for the difference between two groups. Using the lecture's rule of thumb, how should you read this?
opts: The observed effect is unlikely to be due to chance, so the null is rejected
The study had a biased procedure
why: p < .05 means the effect is so unlikely by chance that the null should be rejected.

q: For Assignment 1, a student writes: 'The article suggests future studies test other colours; I will also suggest testing other colours.' Another writes: 'Since the effect was found in the US, a future study should test whether it holds in Malaysia, because cultural norms about clothing colour may differ.' Which approach follows the lecture's rules?
opts: The first, because it stays faithful to the article
The second, because it is the student's own justified idea that builds on the findings
Neither, because Assignment 1 does not ask for future research
why: Future research must be your own idea that logically extends the findings, with a justification; restating the article's suggestion earns ZERO for that section.

q: When evaluating a Methods section, which question is the lecture's?
opts: Is the research question new and relevant?
Did the authors discuss practical implications?
Are the results consistent with past research?
Are the measures used representative of the variables?
why: Methods evaluation asks about appropriate data collection, representative measures and unbiased procedures.

q: A reviewer asks: 'Did the authors consider alternative explanations for their findings?' Which section is being evaluated?
why: Evaluating the Discussion includes whether relevant literature and alternative explanations were discussed.

q: Study 1: coffee drinkers spotted FEWER errors than non-drinkers, yet the authors conclude 'the hypothesis is supported.' Where is the flaw?
opts: Results – the conclusion contradicts the finding
Method – there was no eye tracking
why: A Results evaluation asks whether conclusions drawn from results are fair and logical; here they are not.

q: Study 3's literature says highly self-aware people are LESS susceptible to misattributing emotions, but the hypothesis predicts a NEGATIVE relationship between self-awareness and identifying emotions. Which question from the lecture flags this flaw?
opts: Does the theoretical framework justify the hypotheses?
why: The framework implies a positive relationship, so it does not justify the stated hypothesis (an Introduction/framework flaw).

q: Study 2 reviews research on employees' commitment to their organisation, then surveys 345 psychology students. Which section's evaluation question best identifies this problem?
opts: Methods: is this an appropriate way to collect data and are measures representative of the variables?
Results: are results consistent with past research?
Introduction: does each point flow to the next?
why: The sample does not match the population and variables described in the literature, which is a Methods issue.

q: Study 4's hypothesis compares couples who stay off Facebook with couples who keep using it, but all 64 couples were simply measured twice. What is the main methods problem?
opts: Trust was measured by both partners
There was no comparison group of couples who continued using Facebook
The sample size was too large
why: Without a group that kept using Facebook, the method cannot test the comparison stated in the hypothesis.

q: A paper's Discussion states: 'Our finding that gratitude predicts sleep quality mirrors earlier work on positive emotions and health, placing it within a broader pattern in wellbeing research.' Which purpose of the Discussion is this?
why: Linking back to broader literature gives a 'big picture' view by relating the findings to research within the topic area.

q: Academic writing is best defined as:
opts: The formal and logical expression of intellectual information
Any writing that uses technical jargon
Writing that expresses the author's personal feelings
why: Lecture 4 defines academic writing as the formal and logical expression of intellectual information, objective in tone.

q: According to Lecture 4, in university your writing is an indication of:
why: In high school writing indicates understanding; in university it indicates the quality of your thoughts.

q: Which is NOT a typical audience for academic writing?
why: The lecture states the typical audience will NOT be your course mates or friends.

q: Which of the following is a FUNCTION word?
why: Function words (articles, prepositions, conjunctions) connect words but carry no meaning by themselves.

q: A 20-word paragraph contains 12 content words. What is its lexical density?
why: Lexical density = content words ÷ total words × 100 = 12/20 × 100 = 60%.

q: Interview transcripts and spoken language typically have a lexical density of about:
why: Spoken language is about 45%; fiction 48–51%; expository writing 55–58%.

q: A text that sounds vague, hesitant and uses far more words than needed most likely has:
why: Very low lexical density texts can seem meaningless, vague or hesitant and excessively verbose.

q: High lexical density is acceptable in academic writing when:
opts: All specialist terms, constructs and variables have been clearly defined
The writer uses many personal pronouns
why: High density is acceptable if all specialist terms are clearly defined.

q: A student writes: 'This literature review will discuss studies on sleep.' What problem does this show?
why: Telegraphing announces what the text will do ('This review will show…') and should be removed.

q: 'Many people believe that social media harms teens' is an example of:
why: Weasel words are ambiguous, misleading phrases like 'Many people believe that…'.

q: Which revision best applies nominalization to 'Teenagers are increasingly getting involved in promiscuous behaviour, and they could catch and spread STDs'?
opts: Teens are getting involved and catching STDs
Promiscuity among teens presents a sexual health concern
We found that teens spread STDs
It is a fact that teenagers spread STDs
why: Nominalization turns verb phrases (actions) into nouns (concepts): 'promiscuity', 'sexual health concern'.

q: Nominalization involves:
why: Nominal style turns verbs into nouns to create a more convincing, confident tone.

q: Which sentence uses impersonal construction?
opts: The researcher handed out the questionnaires
The questionnaires were then administered to the participants
why: Impersonal construction backgrounds the author and participants, often using the passive voice.

q: A group of five students writes up their study. Following Lecture 4's advice, they should refer to themselves as:
why: In group research, impersonal construction means using 'the researchers' or 'the research team' instead of 'we/us'.

q: Which sentence uses the most appropriate hedging language?
opts: These findings prove that social support determines stress
It is a fact that social support always reduces stress
These findings suggest that social support may predict academic stress
why: Hedging uses cautious words such as 'suggest' and 'may'; 'prove', 'fact', 'always' and 'must' imply certainty.

q: Using hedging language shows that the writer:
opts: Is unsure about their topic and lacks knowledge
Is open to revising conclusions with new evidence and acknowledges potential bias
why: Hedging indicates tentativeness, openness to new evidence, and acknowledgement of possible bias or inaccuracy.

q: 'There were 50 men and 50 girls, aged 18–25.' What is the best revision according to Lecture 4?
opts: There were 50 boys and 50 girls, aged 18–25
There were 100 people, aged 18–25, mostly men
There were 50 gentlemen and 50 ladies, aged 18–25
There were 50 men and 50 women, aged 18–25
why: Avoid biased (e.g. sexist) wording; adult females should be called women, parallel to men.

q: Which is NOT listed in Lecture 4 as a benefit of reading broadly?
opts: Learning good pacing, phrasing and structure by example
Guaranteeing a higher lexical density in every sentence
Helping you develop your own author writing voice
why: Reading improves language, vocabulary, structure and writing voice; the lecture does not claim it guarantees higher lexical density.

q: A student surveys 200 adults and finds that people who sleep less report more stress. Which sentence is most appropriate for the results section?
opts: Lack of sleep causes higher stress.
Sleep duration was negatively associated with stress.
Sleep has a strong impact on stress.
why: Causal words (cause, increase, impact) are only appropriate for experiments; correlational survey studies should use 'associated with' or 'negative relationship between'.

q: In scientific writing, 'significant' most closely means:
opts: Important or meaningful to the reader
A difference or relationship between variables indicated by a valid statistical test
Large enough to have practical influence
why: The lecture defines 'significant' as a statistically significant difference or relationship shown by a valid statistical test (e.g. t-test, ANOVA).

q: A questionnaire gives very similar scores when the same participants complete it twice, two weeks apart. This describes its:
why: Reliability refers to whether the design/measures return consistent results.

q: A researcher uses a measure of shoe size to answer a question about intelligence. The main problem is with:
why: Validity is the use of appropriate procedures, measures or techniques for answering a research question.

q: Why does the lecture recommend citing an academic article rather than a dictionary when defining terms?
opts: Dictionaries are always out of date
Dictionary definitions are not conceptual definitions
Dictionaries do not include psychology words
why: The lecture notes that dictionary definitions are NOT conceptual definitions, so academic sources should be used.

q: Which is the correct order of the drafting process?
opts: Outline, free writing, first draft, editing, revising, polishing
Free writing, outline, first draft, revising, editing, polishing
Free writing, first draft, outline, editing, polishing, revising
First draft, outline, free writing, revising, polishing, editing
why: The six steps are free writing, develop an outline, first draft, redrafting/revising, editing, polishing.

q: Mei is writing her first draft and keeps stopping to fix grammar and check the word count. Based on the lecture, what advice fits best?
opts: Keep writing freely; poor writing is better than no writing
Stop and fix every sentence before moving on
Cut the draft to the word limit before continuing
Return to free writing and list more theories
why: In the first draft you flesh out ideas freely without worrying about grammar or word limit: 'Poor writing > No writing'.

q: Asking 'Is more evidence needed for this point?' and 'Who might disagree with this?' belongs mainly to which stage?
why: Revising involves checking clarity, logical order, and whether arguments need more justification, and considering who might agree or disagree.

q: Checking formatting, punctuation and errors like 'an' vs 'and' is part of:
why: Polishing focuses on formatting, minor spelling/grammar errors and punctuation – 'the devil is in the details'.

q: According to the lecture, which statement about editing is correct?
opts: Editing usually takes less time than the initial writing
You should add material during editing to reach the word count
Editing usually takes longer and requires more attention than initial writing
why: The lecture states editing usually takes longer and requires more attention; fluff should never be added to raise word count.

q: In the sandwich structure, what is the job of the concluding sentence?
opts: Introduce the general point of the paragraph
Provide a reference supporting the claim
Explain relevance to the broader argument and connect to the next idea
Summarize every study cited so far
why: The last/concluding sentence explains the paragraph's relevance and how it connects to the next idea.

q: 'Their diet consists mainly of smaller fish and aquatic plants (Thompson, 2014).' In the piranha paragraph, this sentence is part of the:
why: The elaboration of point provides evidence, with a reference, supporting the topic sentence that piranhas are relatively harmless.

q: Which paragraph best follows the lecture's guidelines?
opts: One sentence stating a key finding
Four sentences all developing one point, ending with a link to the next idea
Twelve sentences covering three different theories
A full page without breaks so the argument is not interrupted
why: Good paragraphs are usually 3–5 sentences on one point; single sentences are not paragraphs and no paragraphing creates a 'Massive Death Wall of Text'.

q: An email to your lecturer requesting an extension falls where on the formality spectrum?
why: Messages to persons-in-charge, supervisors and lecturers are 'somewhat formal'; highly formal is for legal documents and policies.

q: You are emailing a Western professor who signed their reply with just their first name. What does the lecture advise?
opts: Switch to first name and emojis immediately
Keep addressing the recipient formally to stay on the safe side
Use Malaysian suffixes like '-lah' to sound friendly
why: Although Western recipients tend to be less formal, it is advisable to keep addressing them formally – you never know who the email may be forwarded to.

q: Which first email is most likely to get a reply according to the lecture?
opts: A 300-word email with a 90-character subject line
A 75–100 word email with a subject line under 50 characters
A one-line email with no subject
A 500-word email explaining your full background
why: Research cited in the lecture suggests emails of 75–100 words are most likely to get a response, and effective subject lines are under 50 characters.

q: When emailing your own lecturer, how should you introduce yourself?
opts: Your nickname and your Instagram handle
why: For your own lecturer the recommended format is full name, student ID number and class/subject name.

q: Which best describes a literature review according to the lecture?
opts: An assessment or evaluation of existing research to identify grounds for further research
A summary of every study ever published on a topic
A list of references in APA format
A report of new data collected by the author
why: Literature + review = an assessment or evaluation of existing research with the purpose of identifying grounds for further research.

q: Which is NOT one of the functions of a literature review in the APA definition?
opts: Defines and clarifies the topic or problem
Suggests the next step in addressing the problem
Reports the statistical results of a new experiment
why: The APA definition covers defining the topic, summarizing previous investigations, identifying relations/gaps/inconsistencies, and suggesting next steps – not reporting new results.

q: Jun's literature review clearly defines his variables and cites many studies, but never explains why the variables should be related. What is missing?
opts: A theoretical framework showing logical connections between variables
why: A good literature review shows logical connections between variables via a strong theoretical framework, alongside definitions, evidence and importance.

q: What is the correct order of the initial stages of conducting a literature review?
opts: Quick read, define search scope, critical reading, decide on relevance, extract and organize
Critical reading, quick read, extract and organize, decide on relevance, define search scope
Define search scope and initial search, quick read, decide on relevance, critical reading, extract and organize
Define search scope, critical reading, quick read, extract and organize, decide on relevance
why: The lecture's sequence is search scope/initial search, quick read, relevance, critical reading, then extract and organize.

q: Aisha only knows she likes developmental psychology and starts reading a textbook to find questions that interest her. This is an example of:
why: A broad search reviews a general domain; it is exploratory, giving broad but shallow understanding, and textbooks are a good resource.

q: A broad initial search typically results in:
opts: Deep but narrow understanding of one variable
Broad but shallow understanding of the topic
why: The lecture describes the broad search as exploratory, resulting in broad but shallow understanding.

q: Where are an article's keywords usually located?
opts: At the end of the discussion
why: Keywords are usually placed after the abstract and help narrow your search quickly.

q: You found one article that fits your topic perfectly. Which strategy does the lecture recommend for finding more?
opts: Search only its title words in a dictionary
Scan its reference list and use Google Scholar's 'Related articles' and 'Cited by'
Use only textbooks from now on
why: Using the article's references, plus 'Related articles' and 'Cited by' on Google Scholar, is the recommended approach.

q: Ravi wants to study the Fear of Missing Out but finds very few studies. Which is the best next step?
opts: Search related terms such as social isolation, feeling left out and ostracism
Use only studies published this year
why: For topics with limited research, expand your search area by searching related terms like feeling left out, social isolation/loneliness and ostracism.

q: In a quick read, which part gives a 'bird's eye' view of the research in about 150–200 words?
why: The abstract gives a bird's-eye view in about 150–200 words; the title tells you the variables.

q: During the relevance stage, an article seems only marginally related to your topic. What does the lecture advise?
opts: Set it aside, as it may be useful for your eventual write-up
Cite it as your main source
Rewrite its findings to fit your topic
why: Do not be overly strict at this stage; set the article aside rather than discarding it, as it may be marginally relevant later.

q: Your topic is music therapy for children with ADHD. Which study title would be considered unrelated?
opts: Diagnosis and treatment of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)
Agreement between teachers' ratings and observations of hyperactivity, inattentiveness, and defiance
Identification and evaluation of children with autism spectrum disorders
Music listening and impulsivity in children with ADHD
why: The lecture classifies the autism identification study as unrelated; the ADHD diagnosis study is closely related and the teacher ratings study broadly related.

q: Which describes active (critical) reading?
opts: Understanding the article thoroughly while engaging with and critiquing it
Reading only the title and abstract
Copying the abstract into your notes
why: Critical reading is active reading – attending to specifics and critiquing; passive reading only grasps the basics or gist.

q: Which is part of the lecture's guidelines for approaching an article critically?
opts: Ignore your research question to stay objective
Read every section with equal attention regardless of relevance
Ask questions as you read and build your own arguments
why: Guidelines: keep the research question in mind, focus on relevant details, ask questions, analyze, and build your own arguments; making notes and highlighting are encouraged.

q: A table where each row is one study, with columns for hypothesis, method and results, uses which approach?
why: The author-centric approach extracts and organizes literature by what each study found.

q: An experienced researcher wants to update herself on the latest findings and write a review paper. Which literature table approach suits her best?
why: The concept-centric approach suits people familiar with the area who want to update on latest findings, and is useful for review papers.

q: Which approach does the lecture recommend for the second assignment?
opts: Author-centric, to dive deep into each study
Concept-centric, because it is more advanced
Either, as long as it is alphabetical
why: The author-centric approach is recommended for the second assignment and for those new to a topic.

q: Late in your search you find a study that has already answered your research question. According to the lecture, you should:
opts: Ignore it so your proposal stays original
why: If a new article makes you rethink your question, or shows it has already been answered, you may need to revise your research question.

q: Which sequence correctly reflects the broad-narrow-broad approach?
opts: General introduction, review of literature, research gap, method and results, discussion and implications
Results, general introduction, research gap, discussion
Research gap, general introduction, implications, review of literature
why: The article opens broadly (introduction, review), narrows to the gap, hypotheses, methods and results, then broadens again in the discussion and implications.

q: For the PSY113 literature review assignment, which section should be left out?
why: Because no data are collected, the method, analysis, results and limitations sections are left out.

q: Which is the best first sentence for a general introduction on coffee and health?
opts: According to the General Aggression Model, caffeine increases arousal.
Coffee is the most widely consumed beverage in the world after water.
Smillie and Gökçen (2010) found caffeine enhances working memory in extraverts.
p < .05 was found for caffeine and heart rate.
why: The lecture advises avoiding research findings or theory in the first sentence and introducing the topic broadly and relevantly, as you would to non-psychologists.

q: What is the main purpose of including a statistic like '400 million cups of coffee are consumed every day' in the introduction?
opts: To show readers how the topic influences their lives and set the context
why: Statistics help tell readers how the topic affects their lives and describe the context of interest for the study.

q: According to the lecture, a theoretical framework is best defined as:
opts: The explanation for the connections between variables
A formally named theory published in a textbook
A list of all studies on a topic
The hypotheses of the current study
why: A theoretical framework is the explanation for the connections between variables and does not need to be a formal model or theory.

q: A student wants to explain why heavy Facebook users see others as happier by using the availability heuristic. This presents a theoretical framework using:
why: The lecture's Facebook example (Chou & Edge, 2012) illustrates a theoretical framework presented using a concept – the availability heuristic.

q: What does the lecture recommend about the number of theoretical frameworks for a first literature review?
opts: Use at least three to show breadth
Choose only one for a parsimonious explanation
Use as many as the word count allows
why: Using multiple frameworks is a fairly advanced skill; it is highly recommended to choose only ONE for a parsimonious explanation.

q: Without citing supporting research, a theoretical framework will:
opts: Seem more original and therefore stronger
Sound like a personal opinion and be called into question
Be accepted if it is logical
why: Citations give weight and continuity; without evidence the framework sounds like personal opinion and arguments get questioned.

q: Which should be EXCLUDED when describing a past study in your literature review?
opts: A brief argument for why the study is relevant
why: Exclude inferential statistics, detailed procedures/measures and the study's own implications; include authors, brief description, key findings and relevance.

q: A sentence lists eleven citations in brackets to show that caffeine affects heart rate, breathing and wakefulness. What is the lecture's view?
opts: Excellent – many citations show deep reading
It is required for a strong theoretical framework
It is acceptable only in the introduction
This is citation spamming; many citations are not an indication of deep reading
why: The lecture warns against spamming citations; a focused source such as one meta-analysis is preferred.

q: A past study is relevant to supporting your theoretical framework if it:
opts: Was published in the same country as you
Establishes a direction of causality between your variables of interest
Uses exactly the same sample size you plan to use
Has the most citations on Google Scholar
why: Relevant studies claim a relationship between the variables, establish causal direction, explain why variables are related, or support/disprove the framework.

q: A proposed study replicates the lead paper and logically extends it by adding one new variable. Its research gap is best classified as:
why: A moderately-strong gap proposes a replication and logical extension from the lead paper, or compares two competing methods/models.

q: A student proposes to study exactly what the lead article listed under 'suggestions for future research'. This gap is most likely:
why: A weak gap has minimal potential to add/challenge understanding and may simply be a future-research suggestion already mentioned in the lead article.

q: Which justification for a new study does the lecture say is NOT enough?
opts: It may help create a new theoretical model
It addresses an obvious and important gap in the area
It repeats a published study using a Malaysian sample
why: Merely conducting the same study with a different/larger sample, gender, age or a Malaysian sample is NOT enough of a contribution.

q: 'The findings may extend Jones and Lejuez (2005), who found caffeine consumption associated with sensation seeking.' This is an example of a:
why: Strong theoretical implications go beyond 'adding understanding' by refining or extending specific existing theories and studies.

q: Which practical implication best follows the lecture's 'Do' list?
opts: This study will contribute knowledge about coffee.
This study will end all diet-related illness worldwide.
Coffee intake guidelines could be tailored to personality, e.g. differing recommendations for extraverts and introverts.
People will know coffee affects their health.
why: Practical implications should be specific to the study and linked to its theoretical framework, not vague ('contribute knowledge') or overly grand.

q: A study on encouraging hotel guests to use less energy-intensive air-conditioner settings is presented in the lecture to illustrate:
opts: Linking research to the Sustainable Development Goals
why: The SDG activity asks students to identify which SDGs studies like this one (reducing carbon emissions) may contribute to.

q: When assessing the flow of a literature review outline, which question does the lecture suggest asking?
opts: How many citations does each point have?
Does each point include a p-value?
Would someone ask 'Why is this here?'
why: Assess whether the flow makes sense, whether parts are out of place, and whether a reader would ask 'Why is this here?' or 'What was the point of this?'

q: Which term means giving credit to an idea that is not yours and telling readers where it came from?
why: The lecture defines citation as referring to or giving credit to an idea that is not yours, telling readers where it originated.

q: According to the lecture, which of the following is TRUE about plagiarism?
opts: It can be deliberate or accidental
It only counts if it is deliberate
It only applies to direct quotes
It is acceptable if you change a few words
why: Plagiarism can be either deliberate or accidental; minor word changes still count.

q: A student copies a sentence from a journal article, swaps three words for synonyms, and adds no citation. What is this?
why: Using synonyms to change a few words and not citing are both listed as things that count as plagiarism.

q: Copying how many words in a sequence without a citation will lead to suspicions of plagiarism?
why: The lecture says copying three or more words in a sequence without a citation counts as plagiarism.

q: What does the 'A' in the RAP strategy stand for?
opts: Ask for the main idea and supporting evidence
why: RAP = Read the original, Ask for the main idea and evidence, Put it in your own words.

q: Mei remembers her notes better when she rewrites textbook ideas in her own words rather than copying them. Which concept explains this?
why: The Generation Effect: we remember things better if we were the source of that information.

q: Which paraphrase attempt in the lecture's 'Good, Bad and Ugly' example was best?
opts: The one that swapped the authors' names and a few words
The one that kept the original sentence order but added a citation
The one that quoted the whole passage
The one that restructured the idea, interpreted the main point and cited the source
why: A good paraphrase uses its own structure and words, captures the main idea and still cites the source.

q: Which is the correct APA in-text citation for an article by Carrie Amber Jones (1998)?
why: Always cite the author's surname only, with the year.

q: Which is the correct parenthetical citation for a 2016 article by Brian Christian and Tom Griffiths?
why: Parenthetical citations use the ampersand (&); narrative ones use 'and'.

q: A paper by Cohn, Fredrickson, Brown, Mikels and Conway (2009) is mentioned for the first time. How should it be cited in the text?
opts: Cohn, Fredrickson, Brown, Mikels, and Conway (2009)
why: For more than two authors, every citation including the first uses first author + et al. + year.

q: Given the citation (McKay & Fanning, 2000, as cited in Brummelman et al., 2013), which source did the writer actually read?
why: A secondary citation implies you only read the second source (the one after 'as cited in').

q: Which source should appear in the reference list when you use (Henderlong & Lepper, 2002, as cited in Brummelman et al., 2004)?
opts: Neither, secondary citations are not referenced
why: You may use secondary citations but not secondary references; only the source you read goes in the list.

q: Which is a correct APA citation for a direct quotation?
why: Direct quotes follow the usual author-year format plus the page number, separated by commas.

q: When citing two sources that support the same point in one bracket, what rules apply?
why: List the references alphabetically and separate each with a semicolon.

q: Fredrickson published two articles in 2013 that you cite. How should you distinguish them?
opts: Add the article titles to the citation
why: Add a letter suffix (a, b, c) after the year, ordered as in the reference list.

q: In a direct quote, what does text in square brackets [ ] indicate?
opts: Text changed so the quote reads grammatically
why: Square brackets show changed text; three full stops show that text was shortened.

q: Which is the best reason to use a direct quote rather than a paraphrase?
opts: The passage is long and hard to read
You want an accurate word-for-word definition of a construct
You want to fill the word count
The source has more than two authors
why: The lecture lists giving an exact definition of a construct, term or variable as a reason to quote directly.

q: What is the difference between a reference list and a bibliography?
opts: A reference list lists works cited in the text; a bibliography lists all materials read
A reference list lists everything read; a bibliography lists only cited works
They are the same thing in APA
A bibliography is only used for books
why: Reference list = all references cited; bibliography = all materials read to write the text.

q: Which APA rule applies to tables?
opts: Use vertical lines to separate columns
Report p-values to two decimal places
Place the table title below the table
Place the table title above the table
why: Tables have no vertical lines, p-values to three decimals, and titles go above the table.

q: 'Brattico, E. (2015). From pleasure to liking and back... In J. P. Huston et al. (Eds.), Art, Aesthetics and the Brain (pp. 303-319). Oxford University Press.' What type of source is this?
why: The 'In ... (Eds.), Title (pp. xx-xx)' pattern marks a book chapter entry.

q: According to the lecture, logic is best defined as:
opts: A verbal disagreement between two people
The study of correct and incorrect forms of reasoning
The collection of evidence through experiments
why: Logic is the study of correct and incorrect forms of reasoning.

q: Which statement about arguments is TRUE according to the lecture?
opts: An argument gives people a reason for believing what you said
An argument is a verbal fight
An argument must contain only one premise
An argument is any sentence that sounds convincing
why: An argument shows what is true and why; it is not a shouting match.

q: Which of the following is NOT a proposition?
opts: Education should be free for everyone
Hypnosis is a controversial form of therapy
why: A proposition must make a claim that can be true or false; 'This bowl of pumpkin soup' makes no claim.

q: In an argument, the claim or perspective you are defending is called the:
why: Premises are the reasons; the conclusion is the claim being defended.

q: A father says, 'You can't borrow the car because I'm your father and I said no!' Why is this argument unconvincing?
opts: Its statements give no justified link to the conclusion
why: Convincing arguments need logic (justified, linked statements) and relevance (conclusion follows).

q: 'Amy will be drinking coffee when I meet her, because she always drinks coffee in the morning.' In this sentence, which part is the conclusion?
opts: 'Amy will be drinking coffee when I meet her'
'she always drinks coffee in the morning'
why: In natural language the conclusion can come before the premises; 'because' introduces the premise.

q: A deductive argument is valid when:
opts: All its premises are factually true
It is impossible for all premises to be true and the conclusion false at the same time
why: Validity is the rule that true premises cannot lead to a false conclusion.

q: Premise 1: Only women can give birth. Premise 2: Alex is a woman. Conclusion: Alex gave birth. This argument is:
opts: Invalid, because Alex may be a woman who did not give birth
Invalid, because only women can give birth
why: The conclusion can be false even if both premises are true, so it is invalid.

q: Premise 1: All roses are flowers. Premise 2: Some flowers are pink. Conclusion: Some roses are pink. Which is correct?
opts: Invalid, because the pink flowers may not include any roses
Sound, because all premises are true
why: Validity ignores real-world facts; the premises do not guarantee that roses overlap with pink flowers.

q: A deductive argument is sound when:
opts: It is valid and all premises are actually true
It has at least three premises
why: Soundness = valid form + all premises true.

q: Premise 1: Israel is the capital of New Zealand. Premise 2: Amy is visiting Israel. Conclusion: Amy is in New Zealand. This argument is:
why: If the premises were true the conclusion would have to be true (valid), but Premise 1 is false (unsound).

q: Which combination is impossible according to the lecture?
why: An invalid argument is automatically unsound.

q: 'If it rains, the game will be cancelled. The game is cancelled. Therefore it rained.' This argument commits which fallacy?
why: Inferring the cause from the result ignores other reasons (haze, power outage) and is affirming the consequent.

q: Why is validity described as 'necessary but insufficient' for a good deductive argument?
opts: A valid argument can still have false premises
A valid argument must always have a true conclusion
Validity only applies to inductive arguments
Sound arguments do not need to be valid
why: Validity is the first criterion, but soundness (true premises) is also needed.

q: A researcher argues: 'Coffee drinkers have better memory. Our participants showed better memory. Therefore our participants drank coffee.' What is the problem?
opts: It is invalid, since better memory could have other causes
why: The conclusion does not follow; as an invalid argument it is automatically unsound.

q: 'Santa's elves travel east to west. Santa controls the sun. Therefore the sun rises in the east.' The lecture concludes that this argument is:
opts: Good, because the conclusion is true
Invalid and unsound, although the conclusion is true
why: A true conclusion does not make a good argument; the premises give no reason to believe it.

q: A student accepts an argument because it 'sounds right', even though its conclusion does not follow from its premises. This illustrates:
why: Believability bias: an argument may sound believable but have an invalid form.

q: Which situation is NOT one of the lecture's reasons for arguing?
opts: To be clearly understood and to understand others
why: Reasons listed: persuade, give reasons/explanations, compromise, be understood. Arguments are not shouting matches.

q: Why does the lecture say inductive logic is helpful in psychology?
opts: It only applies to chemistry and physics
It removes the need for premises
It tells us the degree to which we should believe an argument
why: Psychology has few absolutes, so inductive logic gives degrees of belief and links to generalization.

q: Which statement best describes an inductive argument?
opts: Premises lead to a logically-certain conclusion
Premises lead to a probable conclusion
Premises are always false but the conclusion true
why: Inductive arguments reason from premises to a probable conclusion, unlike deductive arguments, which aim for certainty.

q: Why are ALL inductive arguments considered invalid?
opts: All premises can be true while the conclusion is still false
They are judged on soundness only
why: Inductive arguments are not concerned with absolute truth, so true premises do not guarantee a true conclusion.

q: Deductive arguments are described as 'all-or-nothing'. How are inductive arguments described?
why: The lecture contrasts deductive (all-or-nothing) with inductive arguments (continuum of strength).

q: A debater adds a new premise that overturns her opponent's inductive conclusion. Which characteristic of inductive arguments does this show?
why: Inductive arguments are defeasible: open to revision, objection or annulment by adding or removing premises.

q: Conclusion: 'Amy is very unlikely to place 1st in tomorrow's marathon.' Which added premise WEAKENS this conclusion?
opts: Amy has had a high fever all week
Amy has won her last five marathons while in remission
Amy has never run a full marathon
Most of tomorrow's runners are professional athletes
why: Weakening premises make it more likely Amy places 1st, moving the argument along its continuum of strength.

q: Before adding a premise to an inductive argument, which three questions should you ask?
opts: Is it true, justified and relevant?
Is it valid, sound and certain?
Is it popular, authoritative and traditional?
Is it large, unbiased and logical?
why: A strong premise is true (based in fact), justified (backed by evidence) and relevant to the conclusion.

q: A student adds the premise 'My cousin says expressive writing works' to an argument. Which criterion for a strong premise does it most clearly fail?
why: A justified premise has evidence to back it; one person's say-so is not evidence.

q: In the red wine example, the doctor's recommendation of a Mediterranean diet is an example of:
why: Context is the situation in which the argument is made; a doctor's advice is a more important context than 'everyone else is drinking'.

q: The 'stakes' of an inductive argument refer to:
opts: The circumstance in which it is made
The potential impact of the conclusion
why: Stakes are the potential impact of the conclusion following from the inductive argument; context is the circumstance.

q: A researcher studies 40 university students and argues that adults in general show the same behaviour. This is an example of:
why: Generalizing means observing tendencies in a small group and arguing that others like them will share those tendencies.

q: Which is NOT one of the three criteria for enhancing the strength of generalizations?
why: Stronger generalizations follow logic, an adequate sample size and objectivity.

q: A survey on stress recruits only students who visit the counselling centre and generalizes to all students. Which criterion is most clearly violated?
why: Objectivity asks whether the sample or data collection approach is biased; this sample is biased.

q: What does the 'invisible, weightless, odourless dragon' example illustrate?
opts: A claim that cannot be falsified is not reasonable to accept
why: A premise must be falsifiable; if a claim can't be proven true or otherwise, it is not reasonable to accept it.

q: Which statement is falsifiable?
opts: Vegans secretly hate meat-eaters, and deny it if asked
Everyone lusted over their opposite-sex parent; denial shows repression
The sun rises in the east
Conversion therapy fails; any evidence it works is flawed
why: Observation could show the sun rising elsewhere; the other claims explain away any contrary evidence.

q: According to Karl Popper (1963), irrefutability of a theory is:
why: Popper wrote that a theory not refutable by any conceivable event is non-scientific; irrefutability is a vice.

q: A theory has gathered much supporting evidence and almost none against it over time. According to the lecture, scientists should:
opts: Retain it as a good representation of reality
why: With more support and few disproofs, we retain the theory; it can still be revised if new evidence challenges it.

q: To properly test the claim 'all swans are white', you should:
why: Every genuine test of a theory is an attempt to falsify it; confirmations are easy to find.

q: Which belief was discarded through falsification, according to the lecture?
opts: Your blood type determines your personality
Mindfulness is associated with lowered anxiety
The sun rises in the east
why: Blood-type personality, handwriting analysis, skull bumps and left/right brain are beliefs falsified over time.

q: In argumentative logic, a fallacy is best defined as:
opts: A failure in reasoning that renders an argument invalid
An argument with a probable conclusion
why: A fallacy is a failure in reasoning that renders an argument invalid; premises appear to support the conclusion but do not.

q: 'If we let students use calculators, soon they won't be able to think at all!' This is:
why: A slippery slope asserts that allowing x will lead to a bad outcome y, without evidence.

q: 'Either we stop allowing food trucks on campus, or we bankrupt our own café.' Which fallacy?
why: A false dichotomy proposes only two possibilities when there is no evidence that only two exist.

q: 'A feather is light. Things that are light are not dark. Hence, there are no dark feathers.' Which fallacy?
why: The word 'light' switches between two meanings (weight vs colour), which is the fallacy of ambiguity.

q: According to the lecture, vagueness should generally be avoided when:
opts: Making factual claims in high-stakes situations
why: Vagueness is acceptable for uncertain plans, but should be avoided for factual claims in high-stakes situations.

q: A fallacy of relevance is also called a 'non sequitur' because:
opts: The conclusion does not follow from an irrelevant premise
why: Fallacies of relevance offer an irrelevant premise, so the conclusion simply does not follow.

q: A fallacy of relevance makes a deductive argument ____ and an inductive argument ____.
why: The lecture states fallacies of relevance are invalid for deductive arguments and weak for inductive ones.

q: 'Cooper has never been in a relationship, so he's not qualified to talk about healthy relationships.' This ad hominem attacks Cooper's:
why: This form of ad hominem attacks the person's entitlement to speak on the issue.

q: 'This management style is the best approach to success because the CEO said so.' Which fallacy?
why: Supporting an argument because someone with authority made it is an appeal to authority.

q: Which fallacy is described as the opposite of the ad hominem fallacy?
why: Ad hominem rejects a claim because of the person; appeal to authority accepts it because of the person.

q: '8 out of 10 dentists recommend Oral-B.' Which fallacy does the lecture use this to illustrate?
why: Endorsing a position because a majority or large sample supports it is an appeal to popular assent.

q: 'We have always used lectures to teach at university, so why change to online learning?' This is:
why: Appeals to tradition argue 'this is how it's always been done'.

q: 'If you loved me, you would not have said those things to me.' This is an example of:
why: Appeals to emotion target another person's feelings such as guilt or pity.

q: 'Intoxicating beverages should be banned, because they make people drunk.' Why is this circular?
opts: The premise essentially contains the conclusion
why: A circular argument's premises contain the conclusion, or assume what it is trying to prove.

q: A: 'Free birth control would reduce unwanted pregnancies.' B: 'So you want to encourage everyone to sleep around?' B commits:
why: A straw man wilfully misrepresents the other's argument (safe sex becomes promiscuity) and attacks the distortion.

q: A: 'Cheating on your spouse is wrong; you should tell them.' B: 'But who decides what is moral, anyway?' B commits:
why: A red herring diverts attention by introducing another topic, here the nature of morality.

q: 'John ran a red light. Bill murdered his wife. Both broke the law, so both should be jailed.' Which fallacy?
why: False equivalence presents two things as the same when the equivalence is not logical.

q: A reviewer points out that a drug study's author is paid by the drug's manufacturer. According to the lecture, this is:
opts: A legitimate concern about a possible conflict of interest
why: We may raise concerns about conflicts of interest with good reasons, but should not dismiss a well-supported argument just because of the person.

q: Which is one of the lecture's 'strategies for arguing'?
opts: Ask whether you are being generous with the other person's argument
Avoid using facts to keep it simple
why: Strategies include being generous with the other's argument, using facts, avoiding fallacies and not being verbally aggressive.
